title: Zenlytics x Redwood — Dedicated overload mitigation + remediation SLA alignment
summary: Zenlytics asked how Redwood handles overload on Dedicated (429s, queueing, model/region fallback) and how remediation SLAs will be communicated and tracked. Redwood walked through current Dedicated behavior (admission control, rate limiting vs capacity saturation, graceful degradation options), and the Reliability Program changes: incident taxonomy classification, owner mapping, and new remediation SLA timers (time-to-mitigate/time-to-fix) keyed by severity and tier. We aligned on what counts as an SLA clock start, carve-outs (customer-caused traffic spikes, cloud provider/regional outages), and the comms path (Dedicated email + optional shared Slack channel, post-incident review, dashboard visibility).
topics: Dedicated overload symptoms: 429 vs 5xx, elevated p95/p99, streaming disconnects
Graceful degradation: queueing vs shedding load, fallback model/region policy
Distinguishing quota enforcement vs capacity saturation
Remediation SLAs: time-to-mitigate vs time-to-fix, Dedicated-specific expectations
Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping (required classification in incident tooling)
Customer communications: status page vs Dedicated comms, SLA breach notifications
Instrumentation and reporting: incident-type dashboards and SLA compliance
action_items: Lauren Bishop (Redwood) - Send Zenlytics the Dedicated remediation SLA matrix (Sev0/Sev1/Sev2) and carve-outs language for review - Due 2026-02-10

Rafael Mendes (Redwood) - Share the one-pager on incident taxonomy categories relevant to overload (Overload/Admission control vs Capacity/Fleet shortage vs Routing fallback misbehavior) - Due 2026-02-10
Dev Patel (Redwood) - Confirm Zenlytics preferred escalation path (email distribution + optional shared Slack channel) and update support account notes - Due 2026-02-11
Jordan Lee (Zenlytics) - Provide a 2-week sample of traffic patterns (RPS, tokens/min, burst profile) and current client retry settings for 429/5xx - Due 2026-02-13
Maya Chen (Zenlytics) - Identify which endpoints must never fall back to smaller models (quality-critical routes) vs routes that can degrade - Due 2026-02-13
next_steps: Redwood to draft a Dedicated-specific overload playbook excerpt for Zenlytics (what to expect, recommended client behavior, what Redwood will do first).
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to review Zenlytics burst profile and decide between (a) increased reserved capacity, (b) burst pool, or (c) stricter admission control + queued mode.
After SLA matrix review, finalize comms template language for Dedicated incidents (initial notice, updates, mitigation complete, next update time).
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-06
Start time: 10:07 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Title: Zenlytics x Redwood — Dedicated overload mitigation + remediation SLA alignment

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Rachel Kim, Rafael Mendes, Dev Patel
Zenlytics: Priya Nair, Jordan Lee, Maya Chen, Sam Torres

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer wants clarity on overload behavior on Dedicated and how remediation SLAs will be tracked/communicated.
- Redwood explained difference between quota/rate limit vs capacity saturation, and what graceful degradation features apply on Dedicated.
- Redwood previewed reliability program updates: incident type taxonomy required in incident tooling, ownership mapping, and SLA timers.

Transcript
[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This one is mostly on two things, right—overload behavior on Dedicated and then how the remediation SLA piece is gonna work for Dedicated customers like you all. 

[00:12] Priya Nair: Yep. We had that incident two weeks ago where we saw… not exactly a full outage, but lots of 429s and then some timeouts. And the post-incident review was helpful, but we want to know what to expect the next time.

[00:27] Lauren Bishop: Makes sense. And I’ve got Rafael from SRE here, Rachel from CS/comms, and Dev from Support escalation mapping. 

[00:35] Jordan Lee: Great. Jordan here, I run SRE at Zenlytics. Maya is our platform lead. Sam is hands-on with the SDK and retry logic.

[00:45] Lauren Bishop: Perfect. So, quick agenda: (1) define the overload failure modes we see—429 versus 5xx, latency, streaming resets. (2) What graceful degradation means in Dedicated. (3) Remediation SLAs—what we measure, when the clock starts/stops, what carve-outs exist. Then we’ll do next steps.

[01:07] Maya Chen: Works.

[01:09] Lauren Bishop: Cool. Jordan, can you recap the symptoms from your side? Like, what did you see in app metrics.

[01:15] Jordan Lee: Yeah. So we were doing an internal launch, traffic spiked, and we saw p95 jump from ~700ms to like 4–6 seconds. Then we started getting 429s. The confusing part is some 500s also appeared. And streaming responses were… clients reported disconnects.

[01:35] Sam Torres: To be precise, some were 504 gateway timeouts. Some were 429 “over capacity” in the body. The SDK retried, but then it made it worse.

[01:46] Lauren Bishop: Yep. That pattern is pretty common. Rafael, you want to frame how we classify those now?

[01:52] Rafael Mendes: Sure. Internally we’re standardizing incident classification. So for overload we try to separate:
- Quota/rate-limit enforcement (expected 429s, policy-driven)
- Capacity saturation on the serving fleet (queueing grows, latency climbs, then timeouts)
- Routing/fallback misbehavior (we intended to shed or route around but policy didn’t behave)
- And sometimes a runtime regression can look like overload because throughput collapses.

[02:20] Jordan Lee: Right, and for Dedicated… does fallback even apply? Because we thought Dedicated means no shared pool.

[02:27] Lauren Bishop: Great question. Dedicated means your primary serving pool is isolated. But there are still “degradation” options depending on what you choose:
1) Admission control: return 429 quickly when concurrency is above safe thresholds.
2) Queued mode: allow requests to queue up to a max queue time, then timeout.
3) Optional burst capacity: a pre-negotiated extra pool, still isolated, but not always-on.
4) Optional fallback: typically fallback is more of a Hosted concept, but some Dedicated customers choose a policy where if your dedicated pool is unhealthy, we can temporarily route to an agreed backup model or region. That’s opt-in and we align on data and latency constraints.

[03:06] Priya Nair: We’re interested in (1) and (2). We’re skeptical of fallback to hosted, from a privacy perspective.

[03:12] Rachel Kim: And that’s totally reasonable. For most Dedicated we keep it in-tier: another dedicated pool, or a backup region under your account. Not “random shared.”

[03:22] Sam Torres: In that event, would the response headers tell us we were served by a different region? Because for compliance we log that.

[03:28] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we can expose a region and “served-by” metadata. I need to double-check the exact header name, but we do have that signal.

[03:38] Rafael Mendes: And the other thing is we’re adding structured “fallback_reason” enums in routing. That’s more for our internal systems, but it helps us separate capacity from policy from health checks.

[03:52] Maya Chen: Okay. Coming back—during the spike, we couldn’t tell if 429 was our quota, or your capacity limit, or something else.

[04:02] Dev Patel: That’s a comms gap we see a lot. We’re trying to standardize the error payloads so 429 has a reason code like “rate_limit_quota” versus “admission_control_capacity” versus “upstream_timeout.” Not everything is live yet, but it’s a direction.

[04:18] Sam Torres: That would help. Our retry policy right now is the same for all 429s.

[04:23] Lauren Bishop: Yeah, and for admission control 429s, aggressive retry can amplify. We generally recommend exponential backoff with jitter, and a client-side max in-flight cap. For your use case, we might also set a “retry-after” header.

[04:41] Jordan Lee: So, in Dedicated overload, what is Redwood’s default behavior today? Shed load or queue?

[04:48] Lauren Bishop: Default is admission control first to protect tail latency and prevent cascading failures. Queue exists but it’s conservative. The reason is long queues create “everyone is slow,” which looks worse than “some get 429 quickly.” But we can tune this based on your product needs.

[05:09] Priya Nair: Our product team would rather fail fast than hang. So that’s fine. But the incident looked like it started as slow, then failed.

[05:18] Rafael Mendes: That’s usually the ramp. When utilization climbs, you see p95 drift first, then timeouts, then 5xx/504 once upstreams hit their deadline. Admission control thresholds should kick in earlier to avoid the “slow then dead” effect.

[05:36] Maya Chen: Was that threshold too high for us?

[05:39] Lauren Bishop: Potentially. We can review your concurrency and max batch settings. Dedicated has a tradeoff: you can push throughput, but it increases risk of queueing collapse.

[05:52] Jordan Lee: Can you say that again—batch settings? Like continuous batching?

[05:56] Lauren Bishop: Yeah. Under the hood, we use dynamic batching / continuous batching. It’s great for throughput, but under burst load, if request sizes vary a lot, it can create jitter. So we sometimes cap max batch or separate routes by max tokens.

[06:15] Sam Torres: That’s interesting. Our prompts are pretty variable. Some are 200 tokens, some 4k.

[06:20] Rafael Mendes: That variability is a known tail-latency driver. If you mix them in one queue, long jobs block short ones. One mitigation is route segmentation by max_tokens bucket.

[06:33] Maya Chen: That sounds like something we can do client-side too, like separate endpoints.

[06:37] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[06:40] Priya Nair: Okay, switching to SLAs. We keep hearing “time to mitigate” and “time to fix.” How do you define that, and what do we get on Dedicated?

[06:51] Lauren Bishop: Yep. So the remediation SLA is internal-first, but for Dedicated we’re aligning it with what we communicate externally. The reliability program is making it measurable. Rafael, want to define the terms?

[07:05] Rafael Mendes: Sure. 
- Time-to-mitigate (TTM) is: from incident start to when customer impact is stopped or materially reduced. That can be rollback, traffic shaping, scaling capacity, or routing around.
- Time-to-fix (TTF) is: from incident start to when the underlying issue is resolved, like the bug is fixed and deployed, or the config corrected with verification.
We track both because sometimes you mitigate quickly but the permanent fix takes longer.

[07:36] Jordan Lee: And “incident start” is when you detect it, or when we see it?

[07:41] Rafael Mendes: Good question. For our timers, incident start is when we declare the incident in our tooling (incident-bot). Practically it should be within minutes of detection. We also record detection time and customer-reported time, but the SLA clock is based on declared start so it’s auditable.

[07:59] Priya Nair: That makes sense. But what if you only declare it after we open a ticket?

[08:05] Rachel Kim: That’s part of what we’re tightening. For Dedicated, if Support sees multiple reports or a clear impact, we expect an incident declaration quickly. And the taxonomy requirement forces the on-call to set type/owner early.

[08:20] Maya Chen: What are the actual numbers? Like, for Sev1, how fast do you mitigate?

[08:26] Lauren Bishop: I can share the matrix after this. At a high level, for Dedicated:
- Sev0: mitigation target in tens of minutes, fix in hours.
- Sev1: mitigation in under a couple hours, fix within a day-ish depending on type.
- Sev2/Sev3: longer, more like business day timelines.
I’m being intentionally a little vague on the call because we want you to see the exact wording and carve-outs.

[08:53] Jordan Lee: Okay. We’re not trying to trap you, we just want predictability.

[08:57] Lauren Bishop: Totally.

[09:00] Sam Torres: For overload, what counts as mitigation? If you start returning 429 faster, is that mitigation? Because it’s still an error.

[09:09] Rafael Mendes: Great nuance. For overload-type incidents, mitigation is typically: restoring service to an agreed “degraded but acceptable” state. That could be: stable 429 at a known threshold with normal latency for successful requests, or successful requests above some baseline throughput. We define success criteria in the incident channel. 

[09:29] Jordan Lee: So it’s negotiated per incident.

[09:31] Rafael Mendes: Within guardrails, yes. But we’re trying to standardize the definition so we don’t game the numbers. For Dedicated, we can pre-agree what “degraded mode” means for you: e.g., maintain p95 under X for successful requests, and cap error rate under Y.

[09:51] Priya Nair: That would be helpful. Our business cares more about “user sees spinner” than raw error count.

[09:57] Lauren Bishop: Right.

[10:00] Maya Chen: How do you communicate SLA breaches? Like do we get an email “you breached mitigation.”

[10:06] Rachel Kim: We’re rolling out two things. One: during the incident, we commit to update cadence—like every 30 minutes for Sev0/Sev1 on Dedicated. Two: if a remediation SLA is missed, you get it called out explicitly in the post-incident summary, plus we track it in dashboards. Some customers also want a separate “SLA breach notice” email; we can do that if it’s part of your contract.

[10:31] Jordan Lee: Do we get access to those dashboards?

[10:34] Rachel Kim: Not all of them yet—some are internal. But we can export a report and in some cases give you view-only access to the relevant incident list with classification. We’re being careful on what we expose.

[10:48] Priya Nair: We would prefer a monthly report, honestly.

[10:51] Lauren Bishop: That’s doable.

[10:54] Sam Torres: Can you define severity levels? Like what is Sev0 for you.

[10:59] Rafael Mendes: Yep. High-level:
- Sev0: widespread, ongoing, high customer impact, typically major outage or data integrity risk.
- Sev1: significant impact but partial, or high impact to one major customer/tier.
- Sev2: moderate, limited scope or degraded performance.
We can share the exact rubric.

[11:24] Jordan Lee: For us, if Dedicated is down, it’s Sev0 from our side.

[11:29] Lauren Bishop: Understood. And on our side, Dedicated single-customer major outage is often Sev1, sometimes Sev0 depending on scope and contractual terms. That’s part of the alignment we’re doing—Dedicated gets elevated handling.

[11:47] Priya Nair: That’s important, yeah.

[11:49] Maya Chen: On carve-outs—what if the overload is because we sent 10x more traffic than contracted?

[11:56] Lauren Bishop: Great. So we have a carve-out for “customer-caused incidents” like unannounced traffic spikes beyond agreed capacity, or misuse like infinite retries. That doesn’t mean we won’t help; it means the remediation SLA may be paused or not counted as a breach.

[12:16] Jordan Lee: How do you decide that without arguing during the incident.

[12:20] Rafael Mendes: In the moment, we focus on mitigation. Post-incident, we determine classification and whether it’s customer-caused. The new taxonomy helps because we can label it as “Overload - Customer traffic spike” versus “Capacity - Fleet shortage” etc. There’s still judgment, but it’s explicit.

[12:40] Sam Torres: I like that you’re separating it. But I worry it becomes “everything is customer-caused.”

[12:46] Lauren Bishop: Totally fair concern. That’s why we’re writing down objective signals. Like: contracted TPS, reserved GPU count, traffic at time of incident, and what our admission control limits were set to.

[13:03] Rachel Kim: And if there’s disagreement, we have an escalation path via exec sponsor on both sides. We don’t want it to be adversarial.

[13:12] Priya Nair: Okay.

[13:14] Maya Chen: On graceful degradation—do you support returning partial results? Like stop generation early to keep latency.

[13:21] Lauren Bishop: We can enforce max_tokens, and we can do server-side timeouts. But “partial results” is tricky because it can change product semantics. Some customers implement “short answer mode” prompts on overload.

[13:36] Sam Torres: We can do that with feature flags. But we’d need a signal from you when we’re in overload.

[13:41] Rafael Mendes: That’s another thing we can do—an “overload mode” header or status endpoint. Not fully productized, but we’ve done it for a couple customers.

[13:53] Jordan Lee: That would be ideal. Like, if you’re shedding load, we can reduce request volume automatically.

[14:01] Lauren Bishop: Yep.

[14:03] Priya Nair: What about region failover? If the region is saturated, can you fail over our Dedicated to another region.

[14:10] Lauren Bishop: If you have multi-region Dedicated configured, yes. If you’re single-region Dedicated, then failover is a project—possible, but you’d need a second pool. We’ve seen customers do active-passive.

[14:26] Maya Chen: We’re currently single region.

[14:28] Lauren Bishop: Then your main options are: increase reserved capacity, add burst capacity, tighten admission control, and implement client-side shaping.

[14:39] Sam Torres: On the last incident, what would have been the “best” mitigation in your view?

[14:44] Rafael Mendes: I wasn’t the IC on that one, but generally: earlier admission control, plus route segmentation by max tokens, plus maybe temporarily lowering max_tokens server-side to preserve throughput.

[14:59] Jordan Lee: So you can change max_tokens policy during incident?

[15:02] Lauren Bishop: We can if you agree. We’d treat it as an emergency config change, documented.

[15:10] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable if communicated.

[15:13] Rachel Kim: And that’s where comms templates help. We can say “we’ve enabled degraded mode which may reduce response length” without getting into kernel details.

[15:25] Maya Chen: Good.

[15:27] Lauren Bishop: Let’s talk about tracking. Today, you get a post-incident email. Going forward, we will also have structured fields: incident type, subtype, owner, and whether mitigation/fix SLA was met.

[15:44] Jordan Lee: Owner meaning which internal team at Redwood.

[15:47] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. We’re mapping each incident type to a primary owning team, with secondary consulted. For overload it’s often Fleet/Capacity, but if it’s admission control misconfiguration it might be Control Plane or Routing.

[16:05] Sam Torres: So you’re basically creating a taxonomy.

[16:07] Rafael Mendes: Yes. And we’re making it required in incident-bot. That improves reporting and reduces “misc” categories.

[16:18] Priya Nair: Is this related to your new dashboards?

[16:21] Rafael Mendes: Yep. It lets us see incident volume by type/owner, MTTR by category, and SLA compliance.

[16:32] Maya Chen: Will we see the classification on the incident write-up?

[16:35] Rachel Kim: Yes, for Dedicated we plan to include it in the customer-facing summary, with careful wording. Like “Incident type: Capacity saturation / overload” rather than internal service names.

[16:50] Jordan Lee: That’s fine.

[16:52] Sam Torres: Can we request “no mention of fallback” if it wasn’t used? Our leadership gets nervous when they hear fallback.

[16:59] Rachel Kim: Totally. We can tailor language.

[17:03] Lauren Bishop: On the question of SLAs and overloaded traffic. One thing we should align on: do you want us to prioritize keeping latency stable for successful requests even if that means more 429s? Or try to accept more requests but slower.

[17:21] Priya Nair: Stable latency for successful requests.

[17:24] Jordan Lee: Agreed.

[17:25] Maya Chen: Yes.

[17:26] Lauren Bishop: Great. That makes mitigation criteria clearer.

[17:32] Sam Torres: For 429s, can you include “retry-after” in seconds? Our SDK will honor it.

[17:37] Lauren Bishop: We can. Dev, is that generally supported?

[17:41] Dev Patel: In most paths, yes. I’ll confirm for Dedicated gateway path. Sometimes the header gets lost through proxies.

[17:51] Sam Torres: Cool.

[17:53] Jordan Lee: Switching to SLA carve-outs again. Cloud provider outages. If AWS has a regional issue, does that pause your SLA.

[18:01] Rafael Mendes: We have a force majeure carve-out for major cloud provider region outages, yes. But we still treat it as an incident, and we still try to mitigate—like shifting capacity if possible.

[18:15] Priya Nair: That’s fair.

[18:17] Maya Chen: How about model-level issues? Like a new model version rollout that causes throughput drop.

[18:23] Lauren Bishop: That’s a different subtype: rollout regression / model version regression. Owner is more runtime + model onboarding. And in Dedicated, we can pin versions and do canary rollouts.

[18:38] Jordan Lee: We do pin, but we asked for a patch and then it got rolled out quickly.

[18:43] Lauren Bishop: Right. For urgent patches we may still roll quickly, but we’ll add better canary criteria. Also, that category tends to have fast mitigation: rollback.

[18:57] Sam Torres: That’s good.

[19:00] Rachel Kim: From a comms standpoint, we try to avoid saying “model bug.” We say “performance regression after a change,” and then what we did.

[19:10] Priya Nair: Understood.

[19:12] Jordan Lee: Okay, how do we escalate during an incident. Last time we used support ticket + email thread. It was slow.

[19:20] Dev Patel: For Dedicated, we recommend a single path: pager-backed support line or a shared Slack Connect channel. Many customers prefer Slack for real-time updates.

[19:33] Maya Chen: We can do Slack Connect. Priya, are you okay with that.

[19:36] Priya Nair: Yes, as long as it’s not too noisy.

[19:39] Rachel Kim: We can restrict it to on-call + stakeholders. Updates in-thread.

[19:45] Jordan Lee: Great.

[19:47] Lauren Bishop: Then for comms cadence: for Sev1 we do initial acknowledgement within minutes, then updates every 30–60 minutes depending on severity.

[20:01] Sam Torres: And do you have a status page entry for Dedicated incidents?

[20:06] Rachel Kim: Usually status page is for broad hosted outages. Dedicated incidents are typically direct comms, unless multiple customers are affected.

[20:16] Priya Nair: That’s fine.

[20:18] Jordan Lee: Let’s talk about the “overload” again. Is it always our fault if we overload.

[20:23] Lauren Bishop: Not always. It can be:
- You exceed the contracted baseline unexpectedly.
- Or we under-provisioned relative to what we agreed.
- Or a component degraded and reduced effective capacity.
The taxonomy plus signals help identify which.

[20:45] Rafael Mendes: Another case is “capacity available but not usable” due to a networking issue or control-plane change. That’s not customer-caused.

[20:55] Maya Chen: Makes sense.

[20:56] Sam Torres: When you say “contracted baseline,” is that tokens per second? Or requests?

[21:01] Lauren Bishop: We typically talk about tokens/second and max concurrency, because request size varies. We can translate to approximate RPS for your distribution.

[21:13] Jordan Lee: For our workloads it’s like 1–2k output tokens sometimes.

[21:17] Lauren Bishop: Right, which is why RPS is misleading.

[21:22] Priya Nair: I want to make sure we’re aligned on what we’re buying. If we need burst, we can pay for it, but we need to know.

[21:31] Lauren Bishop: Yep. The next step will be to look at your last 2 weeks traffic distribution and decide. That’s an action item for Jordan.

[21:40] Jordan Lee: Yep, we can share. We’ll anonymize.

[21:43] Lauren Bishop: Great.

[21:45] Rafael Mendes: On the SLA piece, one more thing: we’re implementing SLA timers and breach alerts internally. If a Sev1 is approaching mitigation deadline, it pages the owning team lead. That’s to prevent “silent misses.”

[22:01] Maya Chen: That’s good. Does it notify us.

[22:04] Rachel Kim: Not automatically today. But if we’re approaching a deadline, our comms guidance is to be transparent on current status and next update time. We can discuss adding explicit “we are in extended mitigation” language.

[22:20] Priya Nair: As long as it doesn’t read like legalese.

[22:23] Rachel Kim: Yeah, we keep it human.

[22:27] Sam Torres: Another technical question: streaming disconnects. During overload, we saw more disconnects. Is that the gateway dropping.

[22:36] Lauren Bishop: Often it’s the gateway or upstream timeouts. Under load, long-lived connections are more fragile. We’re improving that, but also recommended clients should handle reconnect/resume if possible.

[22:51] Sam Torres: We do basic reconnect but we can’t resume tokens.

[22:54] Rafael Mendes: If the server can’t support resume, reconnect will re-run generation which increases load. So we want to avoid lots of disconnects in overload. That’s why admission control earlier helps.

[23:10] Jordan Lee: So mitigation may be “cut off new streams.”

[23:13] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[23:16] Priya Nair: Are you changing anything on your side after that incident.

[23:20] Lauren Bishop: Yes. We already adjusted some thresholds, and we’re working on better reason codes for 429 and improved overload dashboards. Also, the taxonomy requirement should improve ownership clarity—so we don’t lose time debating Fleet vs Routing.

[23:37] Jordan Lee: That debate did happen. We were like, who is actually doing the work.

[23:41] Rafael Mendes: Exactly what we’re trying to fix.

[23:44] Maya Chen: How will you classify a “burst pool not scaling fast enough.” Is that Fleet.

[23:49] Rafael Mendes: That’s typically Capacity/Fleet shortage or provisioning lag, yes.

[23:56] Sam Torres: And if you intentionally throttle us.

[23:59] Rafael Mendes: That would be Overload/Admission control.

[24:03] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[24:05] Lauren Bishop: Priya, do you want to talk about expectations around post-incident review cadence.

[24:10] Priya Nair: Yeah. We want a PIR within a week, ideally. Not necessarily a full postmortem doc, but summary and action items.

[24:18] Rachel Kim: For Dedicated Sev0/Sev1 we aim for that. The remediation SLA tracking doesn’t replace PIR; it complements it.

[24:29] Maya Chen: In the PIR, can you include whether it breached mitigation or fix SLA.

[24:34] Rachel Kim: Yes, we can add a line item.

[24:38] Jordan Lee: Also, can you give us what you consider “customer-caused.” Like examples.

[24:43] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we’ll send the language. Examples include: sudden 10x traffic spike above reserved baseline, retry storms, or misconfigured clients ignoring retry-after.

[24:57] Sam Torres: We probably did a retry storm.

[25:00] Priya Nair: Sam.

[25:01] Sam Torres: I mean, it’s possible.

[25:05] Lauren Bishop: It happens. No blame. The goal is to design the system so it’s stable even with imperfect clients.

[25:15] Rafael Mendes: We call it “graceful degradation.” Better to be predictably limited than unpredictably failing.

[25:22] Jordan Lee: So for Dedicated, if we agree “fail fast,” then your mitigation is to stabilize at a cap and communicate.

[25:29] Lauren Bishop: Exactly.

[25:32] Maya Chen: Are you going to add some kind of “capacity remaining” metric we can query.

[25:37] Lauren Bishop: Not a precise number, but we can provide signals like utilization, error rates, and admission control events. We can expose them via dashboards or an API. Let’s scope that later.

[25:53] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[25:55] Rachel Kim: Another thing: We’re updating comms templates to avoid over-specific root causes during the incident. After the fact, we can get more detailed. But during, we’ll say “we’re seeing elevated 429 due to capacity saturation; mitigation in progress; next update at…”

[26:16] Priya Nair: That’s fine.

[26:18] Maya Chen: One more on SLAs. What about “time to acknowledge.”

[26:22] Lauren Bishop: That’s more of an operational target than remediation SLA, but Dedicated does have an acknowledgement expectation via Support. We can include it in the support plan.

[26:34] Dev Patel: Yeah, we track response time to P1 tickets. Separate from incident mitigation timers.

[26:41] Jordan Lee: Good.

[26:43] Sam Torres: During the incident, we asked “is this quota.” We didn’t get a clear answer. Will taxonomy fix that.

[26:50] Rafael Mendes: It should. The incident commander must set an incident type early. If uncertain, they can set “Unknown” but then it’s visible and we review. Over time, unknown should shrink.

[27:06] Jordan Lee: So you’ll have a bucket of unknown.

[27:08] Rafael Mendes: Yes, and we treat it as a problem.

[27:12] Maya Chen: Okay.

[27:13] Lauren Bishop: Let’s also talk about what you can do. Sam, can you summarize your current retry logic.

[27:20] Sam Torres: Sure. For 429 we retry immediately up to 3 times, then exponential. For 500s we retry 2 times. For streaming disconnect, we retry the whole request.

[27:33] Lauren Bishop: Immediate retry on 429 is the one I’d change. Better: honor retry-after, or start with at least 200–500ms backoff plus jitter. Also cap max concurrent retries.

[27:47] Sam Torres: We can change it. Our concern is user-perceived latency.

[27:50] Jordan Lee: But if it prevents meltdown, it’s worth it.

[27:54] Priya Nair: Yep.

[27:56] Rafael Mendes: Also, if you can implement “load shed” in your app—like disable non-critical features when admission control triggers—that’s huge.

[28:08] Maya Chen: We can, if we get a reliable signal.

[28:10] Lauren Bishop: We can start with “if you see X% 429 for 1 minute, flip a flag.” It’s crude but works.

[28:20] Jordan Lee: Okay.
